country.comment: Study conducted in two communities (Mudaka and Panzi) in Bukavu, South Kivu, Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title & Abstract; PDF p. 3, Methods - Study setting

effect_estimate.comment: Descriptive utilization percentages and unsupervised k-means clustering proportions are reported without inferential test statistics, confidence intervals, or p-values; planned child illness/mortality outcomes were excluded due to chart-access and recall data-quality problems.
effect_estimate.value: At follow-up, in Mudaka (n = 287 retained households), 6% of households were monthly Asili members and 46% (n = 133) were Asili service users; across three k-means socioeconomic clusters, Asili usage rose from 20% in lowest-SES Cluster 1 to 65% in highest-SES Cluster 3 (membership: 8% in Cluster 2 and 6% in Cluster 3 vs lowest in Cluster 1), tracking higher electricity access (37% vs 8%), land ownership (57% vs 40%), and maternal secondary-or-higher education (36% vs 18%). In Panzi (n = 513 retained households), 1% of households were Asili members and 43% were Asili users; across k-means clusters, Asili usage rose from 32% in Cluster 1 to 52% in highest-SES Cluster 3 (membership: 1–2% across clusters), tracking higher electricity access (59% vs 25%), cement flooring (54% vs 36%), and maternal secondary-or-higher education (64% vs 37%), whereas land ownership was 25% in Cluster 1 vs 18% in Cluster 3. Qualitative focus groups in both communities confirmed that the price of water at Asili standpipes and clinic fees prevented poorer families from accessing services.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF pp. 4–6, Results (Mudaka & Panzi) and Figs. 2–3

mechanism_certainty.comment: Mixed-methods design ceiling caps certainty at 2. Household follow-up surveys and focus group discussions directly document how monthly membership vs per-use fee pricing at Asili standpipes shaped utilization and priced poorer households out of clean water access, alongside descriptive clustering associations with wealth proxies including land ownership.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 2, Methods - Intervention; PDF pp. 4–6, Results (Mudaka & Panzi)

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines two-tier user fees/monthly membership pricing for standpipe clean water and clinic services (BURDEN: fees), land ownership as a socioeconomic cluster determinant of utilization (ELIGIBILITY: property), and human-centered design stakeholder co-creation of the social enterprise (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION: participation).

outcome_flags.comment: Measures household utilization/access to Asili clean water distribution standpipes and drinking water (water_access) and affordability/price barriers to Asili water and clinic services (affordability). Baseline toilet type was collected for clustering but omitted from reported results due to lack of cluster trends.

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Genuine mixed-methods evaluation combining quantitative pre/post household surveys analyzed via k-means market segmentation clustering with qualitative focus group discussions at follow-up. Although retrospectively registered on ClinicalTrials.gov, there was no randomized allocation and no unexposed control/comparator group (services were open to everyone in both communities and pre-post health outcomes were dropped), making MMAT the design-matched appraisal tool.
risk_of_bias_tool.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 3–4, Methods (Data collection & Data analysis); PDF p. 7, Author contributions

sample_size.comment: Baseline total across the two sites is 1,733 households (2,787 under-five children); follow-up total is 800 retained households (1,191 under-five children). Exact number of focus groups or focus group participants at follow-up is not reported.
sample_size.value: Baseline: 1,733 households total — Mudaka: 843 households (845 mothers; 1,328 under-five children) and Panzi: 890 households (892 mothers; 1,459 under-five children); Follow-up: 800 households total — Mudaka: 287 households (288 mothers; 359 under-five children) and Panzi: 513 households (513 mothers; 832 under-five children); plus follow-up focus group discussions (exact N not reported)

study_design.comment: Non-comparative mixed-methods pre-post program evaluation combining baseline and follow-up door-to-door household surveys (analyzed descriptively and via unsupervised k-means clustering market segmentation) with qualitative focus group discussions in two intervention communities.
study_design.value: Mixed-methods pre-post observational program evaluation (structured baseline and follow-up household surveys with k-means market segmentation cluster analysis and follow-up focus group discussions)
